name: Refugee Status / International Protection

requirements.blocker_text: Well-founded fear of persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, membership of a social group, or political opinion (1951 Convention / 1967 Protocol), or fleeing external aggression, occupation, foreign domination, or events seriously disturbing public order in the country of origin (1969 OAU Convention).
Not convicted of a serious crime, crimes against humanity, or subversive activities -- these disqualify an applicant from refugee status.

evidence_required.document: Testimony/statement supporting the persecution or protection-need claim

outcome.duration_length: indefinite (identity card and residence permit issued to recognized refugees)

sources.title: National Commission for Refugees, etc. Act, Nigeria -- primary statute: adopts the 1951 UN Refugee Convention, 1967 Protocol, and 1969 OAU Convention definitions; establishes an Eligibility Committee (application via immigration officers or UNHCR) and Federal Commissioner decision process, a Refugee Appeal Board (3 legal officers, 30-day appeal window, oral hearings with legal representation), and grants recognized refugees national treatment for elementary education, public relief, and labour protections, plus identity cards, residence permits, UN travel documents, freedom of movement, and inclusion of family members

UNHCR Nigeria -- Asylum and refugee status: NCFRMI (National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons) manages applications; 6-month asylum-seeker certificate on registration; Eligibility Committee decides within 3-6 months; 30-day appeal window

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Nigeria). STATUS: PUBLISHED -- primary hard requirements sourced directly to Nigeria's own National Commission for Refugees Act (a codified domestic statute, tier-1), corroborated by UNHCR's own operational description of the process timeline. Nigeria runs a GENUINE DOMESTIC REFUGEE STATUS DETERMINATION SYSTEM with its own statutory eligibility committee, appeal board, and rights framework -- not merely a UNHCR-mandate-administered process -- putting it alongside Rwanda and Ethiopia as one of the better-documented humanitarian routes in this dataset, with a genuinely detailed legal appeal mechanism (Refugee Appeal Board, 3 legal officers, oral hearings with legal representation) that is more developed than several other countries built so far. Family inclusion in asylum benefits is confirmed by statute; family_can_work is left conservative (false) since no explicit work-authorization-for-dependents provision was found.
